I won't do the full derivation or a training walkthrough here. Your `MISSION.md` lists training models and the math inside them as out of scope. Training would also eat your five weeks and your budget. Here is the short version, plus what I'd do instead.

**What PPO does.** Suppose the assistant tries 100 booking requests. Some end well (right tool, right arguments, booking made) and some end badly. RL nudges the model toward the behaviors that scored higher. A plain nudge can overshoot, and one big update can wreck a model that was working. PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) limits each update with a *clip*. It compares the new model's probability of an action with the old model's, and it stops rewarding changes once that ratio moves more than about 20%. The objective is roughly `min(ratio × advantage, clip(ratio, 0.8, 1.2) × advantage)`. Here "advantage" means how much better an action did than average. The source is [Schulman et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347).

**A correction.** "The best agents are trained with RL" is only partly true. Some labs do use RL on their models. But most agents, including the strongest, are built by *using* a trained model well, with clear tool descriptions, good loop design and tests. That's the part you control.

**What would help your assistant.** Most tool-calling failures come from vague tool descriptions, missing argument rules or no feedback on errors. Fix those first. Then write 20 or so real student requests, each with the tool calls you expect, and run them after every change. That's a small version of the reward signal RL uses, and it costs almost nothing.

What it leaves out: the derivation (policy gradients, advantage estimates, the KL penalty) needs reinforcement-learning basics first.

Two questions:
1. Do you want to change your mission to include training? If so, I'll confirm the change with you and update it.
2. Otherwise, shall I make a lesson on writing tool descriptions and a small test set for the makerspace assistant?
